references.cited_text: THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C106 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ There's a particular kind of week in this city where nothing breaks open and everything still shifts. Y2C106 was that kind of week. The gray hasn't lifted — Noah Tan reported from Lake Merritt on a third consecutive week of overcast skies that have done something to the social fabric of that neighborhood, and it's not a small thing. Toby Lamont told Noah he felt the whole rhythm change. Mina Linas, who monitors the lake and sees who stops and who keeps walking, said even the regulars just nod now and move on. A city under low clouds is still a city, but it operates differently — more interior, more private, more provisional. The benches stay empty. People are waiting for something to break, as Tobi Sobi put it from her kitchen table, watching her kids lose enthusiasm for the outside world.

============================================================ By Maria Keen | Bay Tribune Culture Dimond Pharmacy Draws Dimmed Spotlight The neon "Rx" at Dimond Pharmacy blinked steady against the winter-gray afternoon when word came that Benji Dillon had been spotted there earlier this week. No gathered crowd, no autograph seekers—just the usual flow of neighbors picking up prescriptions and local kids buying candy after school. The pharmacy, with its scuffed linoleum and faint antiseptic scent, isn't the kind of place that usually makes the gossip rounds.

The week's most consequential unresolved story is the Oakland Alternative Response Initiative, and it is genuinely unresolved in ways that should matter to this paper through the next several cycles. Rachel Torres reported from the ground level — West Oakland diners, Temescal bakeries, Rockridge lunch counters — and what she gathered was cautious, specific optimism. Server Elio Perez has been hearing neighbors talk about the white-and-teal vans with something that sounds like relief. Baker Melton Neilon used the word "tailored." These are not nothing. But Torres also named the structural holes: no response-time metrics, no clearance rates, no defined protocol for when a call escalates beyond what the teams can handle, and no named agency responsible for performance evaluation. A program can generate genuine community goodwill and still be unaccountable. Both things are true simultaneously.

The culture coverage this week was lighter in the ways culture sometimes earns. Maria Keen tracked the trace of Benji Dillon's visit to Dimond Pharmacy with the right amount of restraint — scuffed linoleum, faint antiseptic, a small mystery that lingers in the pause before the next customer. Rick Walker, chopping vegetables in Fruitvale, had only heard whispers. Melton Neilon, flour on his forearms in Temescal, was more interested in what the visit said about the city's neighborhoods than about the man himself. That's the right instinct.

Over in Temescal, Melton Neilon kneaded his latest sourdough batch when I asked about the sighting. "I haven't seen or heard anything about Benji Dillon's visit to Dimond Pharmacy," he said, flour dusting his forearms, "but I'm always interested in what's going on in our city's neighborhoods, even if it's not directly in my Temescal community." Rick Walker, chopping vegetables at a Fruitvale kitchen, had only heard whispers. "I haven't seen Benji Dillon around my neighborhood," he admitted, knife tapping against the cutting board, "but I've heard he was spotted at Dimond Pharmacy, which is a bit of a trek from Fruitvale where I live and work as a line cook."

Start with the A's, because the city already has. Hal Richmond put it the right way when he reached for the word "absurdity" to describe a 127-win season — not as an insult but as the only accurate measurement. Benji Dillon threw five and a third innings. Vinnie Keane went four-for-five. Mark Aitken hit two home runs and drove in six. These are numbers that belong in a conversation about memory, not a box score. Richmond was standing on Broadway watching confetti stick to streetcar rails after the 2035 championship, and this week he was watching a team that made that squad look modest. Keane, talking to Richmond afterward, was almost too quiet about it — "coming together as a team," he said, voice steady, which is the kind of understatement you earn at 127 wins. What I keep turning over is Richmond's closing note: stories like this always have endings, and the question is how we'll remember this team when the confetti is gone. That's the right question. We're just not there yet.

By Hal Richmond | Bay Tribune Sports The Rhythm of Late Seasons By Hal Richmond The Oakland A’s won again last night. They always seem to win these days. One hundred twenty-seven times this season, in fact, and counting. The box score reads like a symphony: Benji Dillon’s five and a third innings, eight strikeouts, two hits; Vinnie Keane’s four-for-five with a home run, a double, three RBI; Mark Aitken’s two homers, six runs batted in. The streak grows to two, the record bloats to absurdity, and the city hums with the kind of late-season electricity that feels both inevitable and fleeting.

The Oaks came up twice too, and in ways that don't quite match. Talia Finch went to West Oakland and found Elio Perez and Daniel Cloak and Darius Clark all saying, with genuine warmth, that the team is reaching toward the community and that it matters. Then Simon Leary spent his week with the A's record — 127-35, a machine more than a team by now — and asked the harder question: at what point does the architecture become the story, rather than the people passing through? Martin Richards, a veteran who knows something about being moved across positions and cities, told Simon that value shifts sometimes overnight. Ollie Campbell, who doesn't even follow sports closely, noticed people talking about how the A's keep winning no matter who's holding the beams. The Oaks engagement Talia documented and the A's apparatus Simon examined are two different models of what a sports franchise can be in this city. One is still trying to be recognized by its neighborhood. The other has achieved something so structural it barely needs anyone's recognition.

Outside, the A’s were winning again. They always were. 127-35, another number in a season of numbers. What does it mean when a machine—and make no mistake, that’s what this is now, not a team but an apparatus—keeps running no matter which gears are swapped out? How does a structure like that bear its own weight? Richards, who has no answers because no one does, only the numbers, squinted at the light through the blinds. “It’s not just about adapting—it’s about understanding that your value shifts, sometimes overnight.”

“I feel like we’re really coming together as a team,” Keane said afterward, his voice steady, his words measured. “I’m seeing some great performances from my teammates. It’s an exciting time to be an A’s player.” Keane’s line feels almost understated, a quiet acknowledgment of the machine this team has become. Yet underneath the calm, there’s a weight to his tone—a recognition, perhaps, that this kind of dominance is rare, even for a franchise as storied as Oakland’s. Mark Aitken felt it too, the energy of late-season games where every pitch and every swing seem to carry the weight of something larger. “It’s exciting to see them perform at this level,” he said, nodding toward his teammates.

But stories like this always have endings. Down the road, somewhere an engine wasn’t running, Ollie Campbell considered it all from a distance. “I don’t follow sports much,” they admitted, “but I’ve heard folks around here talking about how the A’s keep winning even as players come and go.” They paused, weighing something in their palm. “It’s interesting how they manage to stay strong like that.” Interesting, yes. But what is strength when there’s no alternative? When the structure is designed to stand regardless of who’s holding up the beams? The record doesn’t remember the moments of doubt, the fractures. It only knows the final weight, distributed across whatever—whoever—was available to bear it at the time.

Meanwhile, Irene Fay, a barista from a nearby coffee shop, sat at the end of the bar, looking a bit out of place. "I feel like community engagement with the Oaks team is something I've heard about, but I don't really know much about it. As a barista, I mostly just focus on my job and don't really get involved in that kind of thing," she said, looking around the bar with a curious expression. Darius Clark, a bakery worker and regular at the bar, overheard our conversation and added, "I feel like the community is pretty supportive of the Oaks team, I see people around here talking about them and it seems like they're trying to engage with us more."

"Tomas? Yeah, he's got this energy about him—like he's always working on something bigger, even when he's just plating up orders," says Le during a rare lull, wiping her knife down. "You can tell he's listening, not just waiting for his turn to speak." Hill offers a different take between loading sheet trays into the washer: "Man keeps his head down on the line, does his job. I hear the podcast chatter sometimes when we're breaking down stations, but Harborline's not the kind of place where you bring that energy to work. We're all just trying to get through the rush."

"Man, juggling the podcast and the line cook gig at Harborline? It's all about rhythm, you know?" Renteria says, checking the doneness of three medium-rare orders with a press of his tongs. "At the grill, it's fire and timing, making sure every plate's right. Then with the mic, it's about catching that same energy but with voices and stories instead of food." Around him, the Harborline line cooks navigate the tight kitchen space—Quynh Le layering roasted vegetables with precision, Jalen Hill silently refilling the fry station as the ticket printer spits another wave of orders.

============================================================ By Nia Rook | Bay Tribune Undocked As the city watched the latest episode of UNDOCKED, Clarissa Dane's words hung in the air: "I feel like there's a lot of uncertainty in the air, and as a District Attorney, it's my job to stay on top of things and try to make sense of it all, but sometimes it feels like the more I learn, the more questions I have." She stood outside a bustling café in Fruitvale, where the sounds of the city filled the background.

THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C105 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ There is a particular kind of week in this city where the news doesn't arrive in a single current but in several, running parallel, occasionally bumping shoulders, and mostly refusing to acknowledge each other. Cycle Y2C105 was that kind of week. You had a baseball team approaching a number that strains belief, a public safety experiment drawing both cautious hope and statistical alarm, a council silence widening into something harder to ignore, and a pharmacy counter in Dimond that somehow kept appearing in everyone's peripheral vision. Let me try to thread these together honestly.
